title: Breaking Enigma
matchup: Turing and Welchman (1939–1940) vs Rejewski, Różycki and Zygalski’s earlier work
question: Does the relationship between the Polish and British Enigma methods support Schmidhuber's claim about priority for their core algorithm?

usual_credit.summary: Turing and Gordon Welchman are credited with the British Bombe approach used against wartime Enigma, rather than with every earlier attack on the cipher. The [National Museum of Computing](https://www.tnmoc.org/bombe) explicitly credits the Polish cryptanalysts with earlier breakthroughs and information supplied before the war, while distinguishing Turing's crib-based approach and Welchman's diagonal board. Colossus was a different machine designed by Tommy Flowers for Lorenz-encrypted traffic, so its contribution should not be conflated with the Enigma Bombe.

works.who: Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman and the British Tabulating Machine Company
works.title: The Turing-Welchman Bombe (museum technical history)

claim.summary: Schmidhuber objects to accounts that credit Turing alone with breaking the German wartime codes and points to the Polish mathematicians' earlier Enigma work. His later summary goes further by assigning the core Enigma code-breaking algorithm to Rejewski, Różycki and Zygalski. His longer discussion nevertheless acknowledges that Turing and Welchman made an important contribution, so the issue is how to divide credit rather than whether the British work occurred.

response.summary: The [National Museum of Computing](https://www.tnmoc.org/bombe) recognizes the Polish cryptanalysts' earlier breakthroughs and the information they passed to Britain before the war. It also says that changes in German procedures made the earlier Bomba inadequate and explains how the British Bombe used a crib-based attack with Welchman's diagonal board. That account supports shared historical credit without describing the Polish and British methods as one unchanged algorithm. Its [Colossus account](https://www.tnmoc.org/colossus) concerns Lorenz traffic, not Enigma; neither museum account is a direct answer to Schmidhuber's passage.

quotes.text: Turing's attack was based on the use of ‘cribs’

agreed_facts: The Polish team developed Enigma-breaking methods before the British wartime Bombe and supplied prewar information: https://www.tnmoc.org/bombe
The first British Bombe began operating in March 1940: https://www.tnmoc.org/bombe
Colossus attacked Lorenz-encrypted messages rather than Enigma and was designed by Tommy Flowers: https://www.tnmoc.org/colossus

Schmidhuber's archived September 2021 article already acknowledges both Polish foundational work and Turing's contribution, although the quoted executive-summary wording belongs to the later 2022 version: https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/turing-oversold-14sep2021.html
crux: Polish chronological priority is acknowledged by the museum account; the disputed question is whether the later British methods are best understood as the same core algorithm or as distinct contributions building on that foundation. A criticism of a single-person popular narrative does not by itself settle that technical division of credit.

card.claim: He says the core Enigma code-breaking algorithm came from Rejewski, Różycki and Zygalski, though he grants Turing and Welchman an important contribution.
card.pushback: The National Museum of Computing credits the Poles but says German procedure changes made their Bomba inadequate, and Turing's Bombe used a different crib-based attack.
card.crux: The question is whether the British wartime methods repeat the Polish core algorithm or are distinct contributions built on it.
